title: Genome-Wide SNP Genotyping Reveals the Genetic Diversity and Population Structure of the Chilean National Maize Germplasm Collection
content: Chile represents the southern limit of the historical diversification of maize in the Americas. Across its pronounced latitudinal and altitudinal gradients, centuries of farmer selection, seed exchange, and adaptation to contrasting environments gave rise to a distinctive set of local races. These races are now conserved in the national collection maintained by INIA. Despite its value as a reservoir of adaptive diversity, this germplasm has remained poorly characterized: previous molecular studies were limited to specific groups or to a few accessions within continental surveys. This study aimed to characterize, for the first time at the genome-wide level, the genetic diversity, population structure, and linkage disequilibrium of the collection, and to establish a representative core collection. 1,157accessions were genotyped as DNA bulks using 20,956 DArTseq SNP markers. The main genetic division followed ecogeographic rather than racial boundaries. It separated a genetically homogeneous northern Andean group of floury maize from a more diverse and admixed central-southern complex. At finer resolution, groups associated with specific races emerged, while some traditionally distinguished races were genetically indistinguishable. Landraces harbored allelic variation largely absent from breeding materials, confirming their role as the main reservoir of diversity in the collection. Genetic inference also allowed accessions with incomplete passport data to be classified. A stratified core collection (n=231 accessions) retained virtually all the genetic diversity, racial representation, and geographic range of the full collection in a fraction of its size. It offers a manageable resource for conservation, characterization, and pre-breeding. These results provide the first genomic framework for the conservation and use of Chilean maize diversity.
